blocks.text: You already got a quick taste of single bracket versus double bracket column selection back in the DataFrame lesson. That was enough to get you moving, but selecting columns has a lot more depth once your DataFrames get wider and messier, which real ones almost always do. This lesson goes deep on every practical way to grab the columns you actually want.

blocks.alt: A single bracket column selection returning a Series versus a double bracket list returning a DataFrame
blocks.caption: The most common early confusion in pandas, worth locking in for good.

blocks.text: 1. Single Bracket Versus Double Bracket, One More Time

df['total'] with a single column name inside single brackets gives you back a Series, one dimensional. df[['total']] or df[['total', 'region']] with a list inside brackets, even a list of one, gives you back a DataFrame, two dimensional. The double brackets are really a single set of brackets doing the indexing, wrapped around a Python list.

code.content:
s = df["total"]           # Series
one_col_df = df[["total"]]  # DataFrame with one column
two_cols = df[["total", "region"]]  # DataFrame with two columns

blocks.title: Watch which one you actually need downstream
blocks.content: A lot of confusing bugs come from expecting a DataFrame and getting a Series, or the other way around. If a later line calls .columns or expects to select further columns, you wanted the double bracket form.

blocks.text: For a single column, df.total is shorthand for df['total']. It reads nicely and a lot of people default to it.

blocks.alt: Dot notation as a shorthand for accessing a single column
blocks.caption: Convenient, but with real limits worth knowing before you rely on it everywhere.

blocks.text: Dot notation only works when the column name is a valid Python identifier and does not collide with something else on the DataFrame object. Three real situations where it fails:

items: A column name with a space or special character, like 'Order Total', which is not valid Python syntax after a dot.
A column name that matches an existing DataFrame method or attribute, like 'count' or 'sum', where df.count calls the method instead of returning your column.
Creating a brand new column. df.new_col = values does not create a column the way df['new_col'] = values does, it just sets a regular Python attribute on the object that pandas ignores.

blocks.alt: Dot notation failing on a column name containing a space
blocks.caption: This is a syntax error, not a runtime surprise, so at least it fails loudly.

blocks.alt: Dot notation on a column named count colliding with the DataFrame's own count method
blocks.caption: This one fails silently and confusingly, since df.count is valid syntax, it just does not mean what you think.

blocks.title: Use brackets when in doubt
blocks.content: Bracket access always works regardless of the column name and never collides with a DataFrame method. Treat dot notation as a nicety for quick interactive work, not something to rely on in real code.

blocks.text: select_dtypes() grabs every column matching a given type, which is genuinely one of the most useful column selection tools once you are prepping data for a model or a statistical function that only accepts numbers.

blocks.alt: select_dtypes isolating only the numeric columns from a wider mixed type DataFrame
blocks.caption: One call to strip out everything that is not a number.

blocks.text: When you have many similarly named columns, .filter() lets you select by pattern instead of listing every name by hand.

blocks.alt: filter with like matching every column whose name contains a given substring
blocks.caption: Grabs every feature_ column without typing each name out.

blocks.alt: filter with regex matching a more precise pattern across many similarly named columns
blocks.caption: Regex gives you tighter control when a simple substring match is not specific enough.

blocks.text: Sometimes it is easier to say what you do not want than to list everything you do. .drop(columns=[...]) removes specific columns and returns the rest.

blocks.alt: drop removing a couple of unwanted columns while keeping everything else
blocks.caption: The inverse operation of selecting: say what to remove instead of what to keep.

blocks.text: Selecting columns with an explicit list also reorders them, since the result follows the order you asked for, not the original order in the DataFrame.

blocks.alt: Selecting columns in a specific order reordering the resulting DataFrame
blocks.caption: A useful side effect of list based selection: you control the final column order for free.

blocks.text: Say you have a wide DataFrame from a machine learning pipeline, dozens of feature_ columns alongside a few metadata columns like customer_id and signup_date. Before feeding this into a model, you want just the numeric feature columns.

blocks.alt: A wide DataFrame narrowed down to numeric feature columns using select_dtypes and filter together
blocks.caption: Combining a type filter with a name pattern filter gets you exactly the model ready subset.

items: Single bracket returns a Series, double bracket list returns a DataFrame, even for one column.
Dot notation is convenient but breaks on spaces, special characters, method name collisions, and cannot create columns.
select_dtypes filters columns by type, extremely useful before modeling.
.filter(like=...) or .filter(regex=...) selects columns by name pattern.
.drop(columns=[...]) is the inverse of selecting, and an explicit selection list also reorders columns.
